cands.name: Kyle Kirkland

money.note: Individuals gave $287,241; PAC money $0; candidate's own money $177,459. Percentages describe itemized individual gifts, which the FEC has processed through about July 2026.

cands.bio: Business owner and former investment banker. Owns Club One Casino in Fresno, is president of the California Gaming Association, chairs the Fresno Chaffee Zoo board, and is former chairman of Steinway Musical Instruments. Harvard and Stanford MBA graduate. Has held no elected office; ran in CA-20 in 2024.

endorsements.text: Fresno Police Officers' Association (listed as his official endorsement on his campaign site)

cands.gaps: We found no stated positions from Kirkland on data centers, land development or growth limits, homestead or property taxes, foreign or investor ownership of land, gun laws, abortion, or school choice and teacher pay. He has never held elected office, so there is no record of official actions. We found no documented controversies, foreign ties, or notable newspaper endorsements. Details on his businesses, jobs created, taxes paid and donations come from his own campaign site and are self-reported. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 survey, and the 2024 survey he completed was for a different district (CA-20). The end of the campaign site page was cut off, so any content after the volunteer section was not read.

cands.bio: Third-generation Fresno-area farmer. Former aide to Rep. John Krebs and chief of staff to an Assemblyman. Served in the California Assembly (1978–1994) and State Senate (1994–2002). U.S. House member since 2005, now for District 21.

controversies.text: Federal records show $27,900 from AIPAC's PAC since 2021; $92,566 from individuals passed through that PAC in 2025-26; 1 trip paid for by the American Israel Education Foundation, AIPAC's affiliate; 1 staff trip paid for by that foundation.
Missed 26 of 676 U.S. House votes this Congress (3.8%), counted from the roll calls through 2026-09-16. Longest run of misses: 3, 2025-06-09 to 2025-06-09.

In 1986, Sacramento police reported that Costa, then a state Assemblyman, and a 19-year-old prostitute approached a woman and allegedly agreed to pay her $50. Costa pleaded no contest to soliciting prostitution. He apologized at the time, saying he accepted "full responsibility for my error in judgment."

endorsements.text: 2026 endorsements listed by Ballotpedia include the Democratic Party of California, the California Federation of Labor Unions (AFL-CIO), the California Teachers Association, IUOE Local 3 and Equality California.
His campaign site says he is endorsed by the Planned Parenthood Action Fund and Reproductive Freedom for All.

cands.gaps: We found no documented positions or actions from Costa on data centers, homestead property tax elimination, limits on investor or foreign purchases of homes and land, growth limits and land protection, H-1B visas, or school vouchers and charter schools. His immigration statements back border security, a path to citizenship and agricultural worker reform. We could not match these cleanly to a stance on immigration enforcement or guest-worker limits, so we left them out. He did not complete Ballotpedia's 2026 candidate survey. His campaign pages were cut off partway, so some of his issue statements may be missing. We could not confirm how his Safer Communities Act claim translated into his own votes. We also found no information on who paid for his attendance at the Yalta European Strategy meetings.

votes.what: Final FY2026 spending package funding most remaining federal agencies through September 30, 2026.

votes.bill: S. 1071 / FY2026 National Defense Authorization Act (final)
votes.what: Final FY2026 defense policy and funding-authorization bill (about $900 billion), carried in the House on the vehicle S. 1071.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Nov. 12 final, ended the shutdown)
votes.what: Ended the 43-day federal shutdown: funds government through Jan. 30, 2026 and three full-year spending bills.

votes.bill: H.R. 5371 (2025) Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2026 (Sept. 19 House passage)
votes.what: House-passed stopgap funding bill to keep government open through Nov. 21, 2025; stalled in the Senate and a shutdown began Oct. 1.

votes.bill: H.R. 1 (2025) One Big Beautiful Bill Act (final passage)
votes.what: The 2025 reconciliation law: extends the 2017 tax cuts, adds new tax breaks, cuts Medicaid and food-assistance spending, and raises defense and border spending and the debt limit.

votes.bill: H.R. 881 (2025) DHS Restrictions on Confucius Institutes and Chinese Entities of Concern Act
votes.what: Bars Homeland Security funds going to Confucius Institutes and entities tied to the Chinese government.
Requires documentary proof of U.S. citizenship to register to vote in federal elections.

votes.bill: H.R. 1968 (2025) Full-Year Continuing Appropriations and Extensions Act, 2025
votes.what: Funds the federal government through September 30, 2025 at roughly prior-year levels (March 2025 stopgap).

votes.bill: H.R. 152 (2025) Federal Disaster Assistance Coordination Act
votes.what: Streamlines coordination among federal agencies delivering disaster aid (hurricane/flood recovery).
Requires federal detention of undocumented immigrants charged with theft, burglary or assault of a police officer, and lets states sue over immigration enforcement.

qual.background: Served 16 years in the California Assembly and 8 in the State Senate, and was president of the National Conference of State Legislatures (2000–01). Has been a U.S. House member since 2005, with Agriculture and Foreign Affairs committee roles. Earlier he was a congressional aide and a Assembly chief of staff, and he is a farmer.
qual.why: Roughly 24 years of state legislative office plus about 20 years in Congress, which is prior legislative office in the high range of the rubric.

pro-life.evidence: Was an original co-sponsor of the Women's Health Protection Act, which would protect access to abortion care.

second-amendment.evidence: His campaign site says that as co-chair and co-founder of the Crime Survivors and Justice Caucus he helped enact the Bipartisan Safer Communities Act. The site describes the law as enhancing background checks for buyers under 21 and helping implement red flag laws.

back-police-order.evidence: His campaign site says he supported federal grants for the Fresno Police Department to hire more officers and is co-leading bipartisan legislation to hire more police in small communities.
